## Overview of Sara_dataset
```{r}
#| width=30
library(readxl)
data <- read_excel("C:/Users/kelde/OneDrive/Desktop/Quarto/Sara_dataset.xls")
data$gender <- as.factor(data$gender)
data$major <- as.factor(data$major)
data$cond <- as.factor(data$cond)
rmarkdown::paged_table(data)
```

This is Sara_dataset, it's a dataset that contains data of `r nrow(data)` subject on  `r ncol(data)` variables.

- In the dataset there are `r table(data$gender)[1]` female subjects and `r table(data$gender)[2]` male subjects with five different type of undergraduate degree obtained (``r names(data[2])``).

- Subjects were divided in four experimental condition from easy to impossible (``r names(data[3])``).

- Everyone describe their fear of mathematics on a scale from 0 to 10 (<span style="color:#FF8787;">`r names(data[4])`</span>) and the number of mathematics courses previously attended (``r names(data[5])``).

- Tests consist in mathematics pre-test (<span style="color:#008777;">`r names(data[6])`</span>) and statistics test (<span style="color:#DE4FFF;">`r names(data[7])`</span>) while subjects self-measured heart rate (normal, pre, post conditions ``r names(data[8:10])``) and then took an anxiety test (normal, pre, post conditions ``r names(data[11:13])``).

## Analysis

### Let's do some descriptive statistics:

#### Summary A:

```{r}
summary(data[, (4:7)])
```
In *<span style="color:#FF8787;">`r names(data[4])`</span>* we can observe **simple relative frequency** from the graph (@fig-graph).

We can also calculate mean and standard deviation to better comprehend this variable:
mean = *`r summary(data[,4])[4]`*, sd = *`r round(sd(data$phobia), 2)`*.

:::: columns

::: {.column width="80%"}

```{r}
#| label: fig-graph
#| fig-cap: "Simple relative frequency of mathematics fear"
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4

k <- prop.table(table(data$phobia))
# "Simple relative frequency of mathematics fear"
barplot(k, col=rgb(0,.2,.3,.7), xlab="Self-reported phobia", ylab="Frequency")
```

:::

::: {.column width="20%"}

![Fear of mathematics test](fear_cat.jpg){#fig-fear}

:::

::::

#### Summary B:

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2,3))
boxplot(data$hr_base, col=rgb(0,.2,.3,.7), xlab="Heart rate base", ylab="bpm")
boxplot(data$hr_pre, col=rgb(0,.2,.3,.7), xlab="Heart rate pre", ylab="bpm")
boxplot(data$hr_post, col=rgb(0,.2,.3,.7), xlab="Heart rate post", ylab="bpm")
boxplot(data$anx_base, col=rgb(0,.2,.3,.7), xlab="Anxiety base")
boxplot(data$anx_pre, col=rgb(0,.2,.3,.7), xlab="Anxiety pre")
boxplot(data$anx_post, col=rgb(0,.2,.3,.7), xlab="Anxiety post")
```

### Analysis of two variables

::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}

First variable: <span style="color:#FF8787;">`r names(data[4])`</span>

```{r}
summary(data[,4])
```

Standard deviation: `r round(sd(data$phobia), 2)`

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Second variable: <span style="color:#008777;">`r names(data[6])`</span>

```{r}
summary(data[,6])
```

Standard deviation: `r round(sd(sort(data$mathquiz)), 2)` 

:::

:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-plot
#| fig-cap: "Scatterplot `phobia` x `mathquiz`"
plot(data$phobia, data$mathquiz, xlab = "Fear of mathematics", ylab = "Score in mathematics test", col = rgb(0,0,1,0.2), pch=19, cex=2.5)
```

Form the scatterplot (@fig-plot) it seem that most of subjects that have a fear of mathematics below point 3 and when the fear of mathematics is high, scores in mathematics test are mostly below 30.

## Conclusion
There's an article about the fear in mathematics classroom [@whyte2012maths], similar to Sara_dataset analyze above, it seems that more a person generally has less fear and higher score on mathematics test; as you can notice there are some missing values form <span style="color:#008777;">`r names(data[6])`</span> (exactly `r summary(data[,6])[7]` NA's). Fortunately, the majority of people remaining did have low *phobia* of mathematics test.
